title: NASA's New Moon Missions Will Hunt Lunar Caves, Ice, and Hidden Hazards
excerpt: Three new PRISM investigations will scout underground shelters, map hidden ice, and monitor environmental hazards — the reconnaissance for humanity's first permanent lunar outpost.
body:
• NASA announced September 30 that it has selected three new science investigations to support its Moon Base program, all aimed at answering the practical questions of a permanent lunar outpost: where to shelter, where to find water, and what hazards await.
  • The headliner is GIMLI, a mission to the Marius Hills Pit that will use ground-penetrating radar, seismic sensors, and a gravimeter to determine whether a 213-by-295-foot volcanic pit opens into a hidden lava tube — a natural shelter from radiation, micrometeorites, and temperature swings.
  • The other two picks: LEMS-SP, an autonomous hazard station for the Moon's south pole that will log micrometeoroid strikes, track exosphere volatiles, and listen for moonquakes; and DISCO, which will make the first in-situ measurements of ice in the Moon's micro cold traps.
  • All three will fly to the surface aboard commercial landers through NASA's CLPS program — though none yet has a confirmed launch date or provider.

The Hunt for the Moon's First Cave

Before humanity builds its first lunar outpost, it wants to know whether the Moon has already built one. On September 30, NASA selected a mission proposal that will peer beneath the Marius Hills Pit — a vertical hole roughly 213 by 295 feet across in Oceanus Procellarum, one of the Moon's most volcanically varied regions — to find out whether it opens onto a hidden lava tube, a formation long theorized but never confirmed on the Moon.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=9mXkcpmIKwY

The mission, GIMLI (Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation), is named for Tolkien's cave-loving dwarf. Led by principal investigator Than Putzig of the Planetary Science Institute, it will combine ground-penetrating radar supplied by the Norwegian Space Agency, a gravimeter to hunt for missing mass where an empty chamber might sit, and seismic sensors — an approach Putzig noted "has essentially not been done since the Apollo astronauts" ran the Moon's first seismic surveys — plus cameras to document the pit's walls. Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin subsidiary, will manage the project and mount the instruments on a commercial CLPS lander and rover, with co-investigators from Boise State, Johns Hopkins, the Lunar and Planetary Institute, and the University of Oslo.

The science case is strong. Japan's Kaguya mission photographed the pit in 2008, and a 2017 study pairing Kaguya radar with NASA's GRAIL gravity data found evidence of a void beneath the surrounding surface. Nearly 300 lunar pits have been identified since, and a 2024 analysis of a pit in Mare Tranquillitatis produced the first evidence of an accessible lunar cavern. On Earth, lava tubes top out around 100 feet wide; under the Moon's weaker gravity, studies suggest they could reach 1,260 feet across.

Why a Cave Matters

A confirmed lava tube would solve two of the Moon's hardest problems at once. The open lunar surface offers no cover: cosmic radiation, micrometeorites, and temperature swings of hundreds of degrees make it brutally hostile. A cave would provide thick rock overhead — natural shielding that would, as one report put it, turn "an intimidating construction problem into something closer to moving into an existing subterranean apartment." For scientists, the tube's interior would preserve a record of the volcanic activity that shaped the Moon.

"NASA Science is building the ultimate interplanetary survival guide to ensure that science goes first to the lunar surface to provide our future astronaut crews with the vital information, resources, and safety precautions needed ahead of time."

— Nicky Fox, associate administrator, NASA Science Mission Directorate

Even a null result would pay off: the measurements would reveal how the pit formed and sharpen understanding of lunar volcanic history. "Confirming a substantial lava tube would give us an insight into how volcanism operated on the Moon," said Gareth Morgan, PSI senior scientist and the mission's deputy principal investigator.

Ice and Hazards: The Other Two Picks

GIMLI shares the PRISM (Payloads and Research Investigations on the Surface of the Moon) selection with two companions. The Lunar Environment Monitoring Station – South Pole (LEMS-SP), led by Mehdi Benna of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, is an unmanned hazard-monitoring station: it will log micrometeoroid strikes — a real threat where there is no atmosphere to burn them up — track volatiles in the Moon's thin exosphere, and listen for moonquakes. The data is meant to keep future Moon Base hardware, and eventually crews, safe.

DISCO (Depth Imager with Spectral and Color Optics), led by Ariel Deutsch of NASA's Ames Research Center, tackles the resource question: it will make the first direct, on-the-ground measurements of ice in the Moon's micro cold traps — permanently shaded regions a kilometer or less across, the smallest but most abundant ice traps on the surface. That data will eventually help NASA turn lunar ice into drinking water, breathable oxygen, and rocket fuel. DISCO will also test how the lunar surface reacts to rocket exhaust and how firm it is for rovers — mundane-sounding work that decides where landers can safely touch down.

The Bigger Program

The selections arrive as NASA's Moon Base program enters its first of three phases. Moon Base I will send Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 1 lander to the Shackleton Connecting Ridge near the south pole to study how engine plumes disturb lunar soil. Moon Base II will deliver Astrolab's FLIP rover to Mons Mouton aboard a Griffin lander. Moon Base III will carry Lunar Vertex — the first PRISM payload — to the lunar swirl at Reiner Gamma on an Intuitive Machines Nova-C lander. All three originally targeted 2026, though NASA has yet to release firm launch windows — and GIMLI itself has no confirmed launch date or provider yet.

"Each new PRISM selection strengthens our ability to deliver ambitious, transformative science to the lunar surface," said Brad Bailey, director of NASA's Exploration Science Strategy Integration Office. For an agency racing to plant a permanent flag before sending astronauts to Mars, the message is that the reconnaissance phase has begun: science goes first, and the caves — if they exist — get mapped before anyone moves in.
